title: Energy Changes and Catalysts
strapline: Why some reactions warm the beaker and others chill it — and how we speed things up.
bigIdea: Every chemical reaction involves an energy change. Whether a reaction feels hot or cold depends on the balance between energy taken in to break bonds and energy released when new ones form.
priorKnowledge: Unit 1: energy and changes of state.
Unit 4: reaction types, including combustion as an energy-releasing reaction.
futureLearning: GCSE: bond energy calculations, reaction profiles, activation energy, rate of reaction experiments and collision theory.

misconceptions.misconception: Endothermic reactions are cold because they 'make cold'.
misconceptions.whyItSticks: Pupils treat cold as a substance being produced.
misconceptions.addressIt: Insist on the language of energy transfer: energy moves from the surroundings into the reaction, so the surroundings cool.

misconceptions.misconception: A catalyst is used up, or is a reactant.
misconceptions.whyItSticks: It is added to the flask like everything else.
misconceptions.addressIt: Recover and reweigh the manganese(IV) oxide after the hydrogen peroxide practical to show it is unchanged in mass.

misconceptions.misconception: Exothermic means it will feel hot to touch, always.
misconceptions.whyItSticks: Pupils use touch as the sole criterion.
misconceptions.addressIt: Use a thermometer for slow exothermic reactions such as rusting, where energy release is real but imperceptible.

misconceptions.misconception: Adding a catalyst changes how much product you get.
misconceptions.addressIt: Compare final volumes of gas collected with and without catalyst — same total, different time.

keyVocabulary.definition: A reaction that transfers energy to the surroundings, so the temperature of the surroundings rises.
A reaction that takes in energy from the surroundings, so the temperature of the surroundings falls.
Everything outside the reaction itself, including the solution and the container.
A substance that speeds up a reaction without being used up.
How quickly reactants are used up or products are formed.

practicals.title: Classifying reactions as exothermic or endothermic
hazards: Anhydrous copper sulfate with water gets hot
control: Goggles; add solid to liquid slowly
Small quantities only; wash hands after handling copper compounds

practicals.title: Catalytic decomposition of hydrogen peroxide
apparatus: conical flask, bung and delivery tube
gas syringe or measuring cylinder over water
hazards: Hydrogen peroxide is an irritant; more concentrated solutions are corrosive
Pressure build-up if the delivery tube blocks
control: Use dilute peroxide only; goggles compulsory
Never seal the flask; check the delivery tube is clear before starting

formative: Predict-then-measure for each reaction in the practical.
Sorting task: eight everyday processes as exothermic or endothermic.
Whiteboard check on the definition of a catalyst.

summative.title: Energy Changes short assessment
summative.style: 20 marks, 30 minutes, including a graph of gas volume against time to interpret.
summative.markSchemeNotes: Credit answers only where the direction of energy transfer relative to the surroundings is stated.

lessons.title: Exothermic and endothermic
objectives: Use the language of energy transfer correctly
retrieval: Is combustion energy releasing or absorbing?
What happens to temperature during melting?

sequence.detail: Recall of energy ideas from Units 1 and 4.
Definitions built around the word surroundings; model the correct sentence form for each.
Four reactions in polystyrene cups; record start and end temperatures; calculate the change.

keyQuestions: Why use a polystyrene cup rather than a beaker?
Where has the energy gone in the endothermic reaction?
support: Results table with a temperature-change column pre-labelled.
challenge: Suggest why the measured temperature change is smaller than the true value, and how to reduce that error.
lessons.homework: Classify eight everyday processes with justification.
lessons.exitTicket: Define endothermic in terms of the surroundings.

lessons.title: Energy and changes of state
objectives: Explain energy changes during melting and boiling
Link state changes to the particle model

sequence.detail: Cooling curve sketched and annotated from memory.
Energy going into separating particles rather than raising temperature; melting and boiling as endothermic, freezing and condensing as exothermic.
Annotate a full heating curve for water with energy descriptions at each stage.
Application: explain why sweating cools you, and why steam burns are worse than boiling water burns.

keyQuestions: Why is freezing exothermic when it feels cold?
support: Heating curve with three of the five sections already annotated.
challenge: Explain why more energy is needed to boil water than to melt the same mass of ice.
lessons.homework: Explain, in terms of energy and particles, why a steam burn is more damaging.
lessons.exitTicket: Is condensing exothermic or endothermic? Justify.

lessons.title: Rates of reaction and catalysts
objectives: Measure the rate of a reaction
Show that a catalyst is not used up
retrieval: Name a factor that could speed up a reaction.

sequence.detail: Prior knowledge probe on what makes reactions faster.
Hydrogen peroxide with and without manganese(IV) oxide; measure gas volume against time; recover and reweigh the catalyst.
Plot both runs on one set of axes; compare gradients and final volumes.
Address the 'catalyst gives more product' misconception using the final volumes.

keyQuestions: Do both runs reach the same final volume? What does that prove?
How do we know the catalyst was not used up?
support: Pre-drawn axes; readings taken every 30 seconds rather than 10.
challenge: Calculate the rate over the first 60 seconds for both runs and express the difference as a ratio.
lessons.homework: Interpret a provided rate graph and explain the shape of the curve.
lessons.exitTicket: Give two things a catalyst does not change.

lessons.title: Catalysts in industry and in living things
objectives: Describe uses of catalysts in industry
Explain why catalysts matter economically and environmentally
retrieval: State one piece of evidence that a catalyst is not used up.

sequence.detail: Four questions on catalysts and rates.
Catalytic converters, enzymes as biological catalysts, industrial catalysts and energy saving.
Structured research task: choose one catalyst and explain its use, benefit and any drawback.
Short presentations; class builds a summary table.

keyQuestions: How does a catalyst save a company money?
Why does using a catalyst reduce carbon dioxide emissions?
support: Research sheet with three sources supplied and a paragraph frame.
challenge: Explain why enzymes stop working when heated, linking to the particle model.
lessons.homework: Complete the summary table for four catalysts.
lessons.exitTicket: Name one industrial use of a catalyst.

lessons.title: Review and assessment

sequence.detail: Definitions and graph interpretation from memory.
Peer marking against a visualised mark scheme; reteach the weakest item.

support: Graph paper and a ruler provided; calculator permitted.
challenge: Design an investigation into how temperature affects the rate of the peroxide reaction.
lessons.exitTicket: Exothermic or endothermic: which do you find harder to explain?
